The main feature of this definition is that we can control:

Online source:
https://generativelandscapes.wordpress.com/2014/08/21/multiple-point-vector-field-example-6-2

Often, what you want to code in Grasshopper has already been done by others before you.
It would be interesting to make a quick online research and find helpful resources.
One of the main online resources for Grasshopper definitions is:
https://discourse.mcneel.com/c/grasshopper/2

OR:

Just search in Google: "Grasshopper [WHAT I WANT TO DESIGN]" and check out the results.

Assignment 6a: Use the definition above to manipulate vertecies and make a similar effect as done with manipulating edges.

C- Manipulating Vertecies:

Z direction:

1- Move each of the 4 vertecies of each panel, with different values, in the Z direction.

2- Make "4Point Surface" from the moved points.


Normal to surface:

3- Repeat the same steps (1) & (2) but now moving the points Normal to surface.

HINT: EACH of the 4 POINTS of EACH SURFACE has a UNIQUE NORMAL VECTOR!

1- Attractor Logic: One of Grasshopper's most powerful parametric strategies.

- Attractor Logic is a very simple design concept based on distances. However the results could become amazing.

- We will build a simple parametric definition below and understand how attractors work in Grasshopper.

- Build a squarish grid of points: S 10, Ex 10, Ey 10.

- Construct a Point and keep in without any INPUTS.

- Use a "Move" component and feed in the Point. Use an MD Slider to feed to direction.

- Change the MD Slider's domains to 100 in both X & Y.

- Get the Points from the Squarish grid and flatten them

- Get the Ditances between the flattened points of the squarish grid and the moved point.

- Check out the distances using a panel.

- Find the minimum & maximum of all distances by using the "Bounds" component.

- Use a "Vector 2Pt" component:
1t Point Input = Constructed Point
1st Point Input = All Points of the squarish grid

- Move all the points of the squarish grid by using the "Vector 2Pt" as translation vectors.

- Make Lines between the points of the squarish grid and the newly moved ones.

- The Lines represent the "Attraction" between the constructed point and the squarish grid points.

- Find below numerous examples of how to affect this attraction effect, by:
- Manipulating vector lengths with commands, such as multiplication.
- Remapping data.

6- Paneling: 

1- Model a non-planar surface in Rhino

2- Use the "Divide Domain²" component to divide the domain of the surface in both U & V directions.

3- Use the "isoTrim" component to make sub-surfaces based on the divide domain² information.

4- Use the "DeConstruct Brep" to extract:
a- Faces (surfaces)
b- Edges
c- Vertecies

5- Now you have a panelized surface.

8- Geometry Morphing:

Another powerful way of panelization is to morph geometry onto a panelized surface, with a customized base shape.

We will use the previous definition and morph a modeled geometry in Rhino.

- First, reference the modeled geometry in Rhino in a "Geometry" component.

- Use a "Bounding Box" and plug in the referenced geometry in the C INPUT.

- Use a "Surface Box" and plug in:
1- Base surface in S INPUT.
2- Divide Domain² OUTPUT in D INPUT.
3- Number in H INPUT.

- Use a "Box Morph" and plug in:
1- Referenced geometry in G INPUT.
2- The first B OUTPUT from "Bounding Box" in R INPUT.
3- OUTPUT of "Surface Box" in T INPUT.

- Note that you can always change the referenced geometry and then reference it again, and the final result will update accordingly.

IMPORTANT:

- If, for any reason, you would need to construct a non-regular surface division (without Domain Division), then you would need to construct Twisted Boxs without using the "Surface Box".

For this purpose, you will use the parameters of that non-regular surface divisions and use the "Twisted Box" component to generate Twisted Boxes, which can then be used for the T INPUT of the "Box Morph".

7- Paneling: Practical Example

Let us use the result from the previous definition to make interesting panelization options:


A- Manipulating Faces

1- Extrude all faces in the Z direction

2- Extrude / Offset all faces Normal to Surface.


B- Manipualting Edges:

Z direction:

1- Move one edge of the panels in the Z direction.

2- Loft the moved edges with their respective facing edges.

Normal to Surface:

3- Repeat step (1) but now the edges being moved Normal to the surface.

4- Loft the moved edges with their respective facing edges.

2- Graph Mapper: Maps a number of values using a function.

- Make a number slider between 0-1

- Make a "Graph Mapper":
1- Right-Click on the "Graph Mapper" and click on "Graph Types" and choose "Bezier".
2- Bring a Panel and watch the output of the Graph Mapper.

- Notice the red line illustrating the INPUT value (along the X axis).
- The Y value is the mapped value of X, following the bezier function.


- Copy the Graph Mapper and start manipulating the X & Y domains by double-clicking on the Graph Mapper.

3- Graph Mapper: Maps a number of values using a function.

- Using Multiple INPUTS:
- Take the previous example and input a seconf value.

- Get a Panel and watch the results.

- Important: The resulting data depends on the order of the values you input. Try to use the "Merge" component to keep track of that order of inputs.

- Use a "Range" of values to input more values.
- Notice that the "Domain" D INPUT of the "Range" component comes with a default domain between 0 & 1.
- Also notive that the default number of steps is 10, illustrated by the N INPUT.

- You can change both the D & N values by contructing a new "Domain" and using an integer slider.

>> Be Careful! If the domain range goes beyond the Graph Mapper's domain, there will be missed output results!

5- Graph Mapper: Maps a number of values using a function.

- Practical Example:

- Use the previous Graph Mapper definition.
- Construct a Point.
- Feed the same INPUT range of the Graph Mapper to the X INPUT of the Point.
- Feed the OUTPUT of the Graph Mapper into the Z INPUT of the Point.
- Check the results in Perspective view in Rhino while selecting the Constructed Point.
- Deconstruct the Point to seperate the X,Y & Z values.
- Build a new Circle.
- Construct a new Point and feed its Z with the deconstructed Point above Z value.
- Feed these new Z values into the Plane INPUT of the Circle.
- Feed the X OUTPUT of the Deconstructed Point into the Radius INPUT of the Circle.
- Check the results in Perspective view in Rhino while selecting the Circle.
- Final touch: Loft the circles together.

- If you have a low quality preview of the loft, click on "Preview Mesh Quality" at the Top Right corner of your viewport and select "High Quality".

- Change the type of the Graph Mapper and check out the results!

4- Graph Mapper: Maps a number of values using a function.

In case we had a domain of values beyond the domain of the graph mapper, we can remap the INPUT values to match a standard (0.0 to 1.0) domain of the graph, use the graph, then remap the OUTPUT values back to the original domain.

Double click to edit panel content…

9- Exercise: Sun Orientation

Start with preparing the geometries:

1- Place a Point to represent the sun Position
2- Construct a Surface and divide it to get sub-surfaces
3- Evaluate the sub-surfaces in order to extract the points and their respective normal vectors

Orientation Method 1:  Using the "Orient" component

1- Build Vectors between each of the sub-surfaces and the sun point (Using Vector 2Pt)
2- Build planes normal to the vectors
3- Orient the sub-surfaces according the planes normal to the vectors

Orientation Method 2: Using the "Orient Direction" component

1- Build Vectors between each of the sub-surfaces and the sun point
2- Adjust amplitude of the vectors to match the original vector lengths
>> These would be used for the Direction B input of the component
3- Use the Centroids of the sub-surfaces as Point A and Point B
4- Direction A: Original normal vectors of the sub-surfaces
